22: photoacoustic imaging and seRs.

24: offer a number of unique properties, including strong resonant scattering and absorption
25: 1, and dramatic near-field 
26: enhancement2,3, which makes them very promising candidates for a plethora of applications. Biomedicine looks 
27: as one of major potential beneficiaries of these plasmonic effects, provided the plasmonic materials used are 
28: compatible with biological systems

33: ing engineered plasmonic nanostructures such as Au-based core-shells (SiO

65: of generating red-shifted plasmonic feature16–21 with a high photothermal conversion efficiency21. Having good 
66: chemical stability and biocompatibility, TiN instruments have been successfully used in biological systems as 
67: surgical and food-related tools, as well as implants22, while well-established surface chemistry of TiN structures 
68: renders possible its easy functionalization by standard protocols23. However, fabrication routes for the synthesis of 
69: TiN NPs are not always compatible with projected biomedical applications. Indeed, chemical synthesis routes24,25 
70: are rather complicated in terms of a number of preparation steps and employ hazardous products, which can 
71: cause residual contamination of NPs and related toxicity issues. On the other hand, nanocrystals prepared by 
72: dry fabrication methods, including direct nitridation of TiO
73: 2 powders26, plasma assisted processing27–29 and laser 
74: ablation in nitrogen atmosphere 17, normally cannot be dispersed and stabilized in aqueous solutions without 
75: applying similar wet chemistry steps.
76: Here, we demonstrate a simple and cost efficient method for the production of stable solutions of bare (ligand –  
77: free) TiN NPs by methods of femtosecond (fs) laser ablation and fragmentation in water and organic (acetone) 
78: solutions. By performing a series of biological tests using 2D cultures and 3D spheroids, we evidence high safety 
79: and excellent cell uptake of laser-synthesized TiN NPs, as well as show efficient therapy effect on cancer cells using 
80: TiN NPs as sensitizers of photothermal treatment at the plasmonic absorption band (650–800 nm).
81: Results and Discussion
82: synthesis and characterization of t iN nanoparticles.  For the synthesis of TiN NPs we adapted 
83: methods of ultra-short laser ablation and fragmentation in liquid ambience, which were earlier used for the 
84: preparation of bare Au and Ag NPs
85: 30–36. In the first “ablation” approach30–32, radiation from a femtosecond laser 
86: (Yb:KGW , 1025 nm, 1–100 kHz) was focused onto a TiN target placed on the bottom of a glass vessel filled with 
87: deionized water or acetone in order to initiate ablation of material, as shown in Fig.  1a (see details in Methods 
88: section). The target was continuously moved at a speed of 2 mm s− 1 during the ablation step to avoid ablation 
89: from the same point.
90: We observed a blue coloration of solution within a few minutes of the ablation process, indicating the for -
91: mation of TiN NPs. Concentration of NPs increased linearly at the beginning of the process and then came to 
92: a saturation after some time. Saturation concentration and time until saturation depended on pulse energy. In 
93: particular, for 100 μJ pulse energy and 5 kHz repetition rate saturation time was 15 min and the saturation con-
94: centration was about 100 μg mL
95: − 1. TiN colloids synthesized by laser ablation both in water and acetone were very 
96: stable with almost no traces of aggregation or precipitation during their storage at ambient conditions for several 
97: months. Such a high stability of colloidal solutions was due to an electrostatic stabilization owing to strong charg-
98: ing of NPs surface similar to how it happens for other materials
99: 33. Indeed, according to our ζ–potential measure-
100: ments, the surface potential of TiN NPs was − 30 mV , which is higher than the stability threshold (20 mV)37 for 
101: colloidal solutions.
102: A typical HR-TEM image of a TiN nanoparticle synthesized by pulsed laser ablation in water is shown in 
103: Fig. 2a. One can see that the nanoparticle had a spherical shape and exhibited a polycrystalline structure, while 
104: the size of single-crystal grains was about 1–3 nm. Interestingly, TiN NPs could have a hollow structure con-
105: taining one or several cavities, as follows from the presence of light areas inside NPs on TEM images (Fig.  2e). 
106: When synthesized in acetone, only 5–10% of NPs contained such hollow cavities, while for the synthesis in water 
107: ambient the relevant parameter could reach 60%. Moreover, most of hollow NPs had only one cavity under ace-
108: tone conditions, while under water conditions they could contain several cavities. As another observation, when 
109: ablated in acetone, all synthesized TiN NPs were spherical and crystalline, while the ablation in water ambient 
110: was accompanied by the production of a certain amount of nanostructured amorphous flakes. Based on our pre-
111: vious experience, the formation of such amorphous non-spherical flakes during laser ablation in water is typical 
112: for easily oxidizing materials (Ti, Fe, Co, etc.). Nevertheless, SAED measurements showed that spherical NPs 
113: prepared under water and acetone conditions present stoichiometric TiN. An example of SAED pattern is shown 
114: in Fig. 2b. Results of analysis of this pattern are summarized in Table 1. Rings 3, 4 and 6–11 correspond to first 
115: 8 diffraction rings of TiN FCC lattice, as follows from the comparison of their positions with data for bulk TiN, 
116: taken from JCPDS database (JCPDS 38–1420). Measured lattice constant 4.272 Å ± 0.114 Å is in accordance with 
117: tabulated lattice constant 4.24 Å of bulk TiN. Rings 1 and 5, which cannot be attributed to rock salt structure of 
118: TiN, should belong to titanium oxide fraction of synthesized NPs. In particular, position of ring 1 is close to that 
119: of (012) plane of Ti
120: 2O3 (JCPDS 43-1033), the position of ring 5 is close to (105) plane of anatase TiO2 and (211) 
121: plane of rutile TiO2 (JCPDS 21-1272 and 21-1276). Thus, SAED data clearly indicated formation of crystalline 
122: TiN NPs with lattice structure similar to that of bulk TiN with some fraction of titanium oxide. Presence of 
123: titanium oxide is in accordance with previous results on the synthesis of TiN NPs by alternative methods
124: 20,23,25.
125: Statistical analysis of TEM images demonstrated lognormal size distribution of synthesized TiN NPs as shown 
126: in Fig. 2c. When ablated in acetone, the mean size of NPs depended on laser pulse energy as shown in Fig. 3. In 
127: particular, the increase of pulse energy from 10 to 100 μJ led to the increase of NPs mean diameter from 25 to 
128: 40 nm under relatively broad size dispersion (25–40 nm FWHM). Such a pulse energy dependence for the mean 
129: size of TiN NPs is in agreement with our previous data on fs laser ablation of Au in deionized water30,31. For abla-
130: tion in water, the dependence of NPs size on pulse energy was not significant and the mean size of synthesized 
131: TiN NPs was always around 30 nm under the size dispersion of 40 nm FWHM. It is important that TiN NPs pre-
132: pared both in acetone and deionized water exhibited strong peaks around 700 nm in extinction spectra associated 
133: with the excitation of surface plasmons over the NPs (solid black and red lines in Fig. 4, respectively). Here, we 
134: did not observe any remarkable variations of the peak position for NPs having mean size between 25 and 40 nm. 
135: It should be noted that TiN NPs prepared in acetone could be easily transferred to aqueous solutions via a simple 
136: centrifugation step.
137: To further reduce the mean size and narrow down size dispersion, we employed the technique of femtosecond 
138: laser fragmentation, which was developed in our earlier works to minimize the size dispersion of bare Au NPs
139: 34–36.

145: Briefly, colloidal solutions of TiN NPs, which were preliminary prepared by laser ablation step, are exposed to 
146: radiation of the same laser in the absence of the target. The laser beam was focused 1 cm below the liquid surface, 
147: while the solution was continuously homogenized by a magnetic stirrer during the fragmentation process (see 
148: details in Methods section). Here, we observed a fast loss of blue coloration of solutions and related disappearance 
149: of the plasmonic peak, while the extinction spectrum of colloids started to be similar to that of TiO
150: x (Fig. 4, black 
151: dashed line), suggesting oxidation of NPs as the main reason of the color loss. Laser fragmentation in acetone was 
152: a solution to the oxidation problem. In this case, we observed a drastic decrease in the size of final TiN NPs down 
153: to 4 nm under a very narrow size dispersion (lower than 3 nm FWHM as shown in Fig. 2d). Here, despite such a 
154: drop in NPs size, plasmon extinction peak was still well resolvable and intense, although it slightly decreased and 
155: blue shifted from 700 to 640 nm (Fig. 4, red dashed line).
156: The plasmonic peak around 640–700 nm for small (4–40 nm) spherical TiN NPs is much redshifted com-
157: pared to Au NPs of similar and larger sizes (520–560 nm), which promises a major breakthrough in biomedical 
158: applications of nanoplasmonic structures. The extinction coefficient calculated by the Beer-Lambert law at peak 
159: position varied from 18 L g
160: − 1 cm− 1 for 40 nm NPs to 6 L g− 1 cm− 1 for 4 nm NPs, which is comparable with other 
161: photothermal agents38,39. Moreover, the extinction peak was very broad and decreased by only 15% from 650 to 
162: 850 nm (Fig. 4). Such optical properties of TiN NPs look promising for their application in photothermal treat-
163: ment (PTT) of tumors and photoacoustic imaging (PAI) of biological tissues.

165: laser ablation, we performed several biological tests. Safety of new TiN NPs was tested in vitro on human micro-
166: vascular endothelial cells (HMEC–1) and on human cancer cells (U87–MG). These cellular models in 2D and 3D 
167: geometries are highly relevant for cancer therapy applications. The viability of 2D cell cultures was evaluated on 
168: Figure 1. (a) Schematics of laser ablation setup. A laser beam is focused on the surface of the TiN target, which 
169: is placed in the vessel filled with a liquid. The vessel is mounted on a moving translation stage to avoid ablation 
170: from the same area of the target. (b) Schematic of laser fragmentation setup to minimize size dispersion of NPs. 
171: Ar bubbling used optionally to remove dissolved oxygen.

# L1 — часть 01 (PDF с. 1–3)

[порождено] Обзор и синтез. TiN предлагается как плазмонная альтернатива Au: у Au 5–50 нм пик 520–540 нм, вне окна прозрачности 670–1000 нм (с. 1). Аннотация: пик TiN 640–700 нм и хвост >800 нм даже при <7 нм; in vitro на клеточных моделях — низкая цитотоксичность и захват; фотоТТ на культуре U87–MG в ближнем ИК (с. 1–2). Это клеточные опыты, не лечение людей. Абляция: Yb:KGW 1025 нм, 1–100 кГц, вода или ацетон, мишень 2 мм/с; 100 мкДж, 5 кГц — насыщение 15 мин, ~100 мкг/мл; ζ-потенциал −30 мВ при пороге 20 мВ (с. 2). Размер: 10→100 мкДж даёт 25→40 нм в ацетоне, в воде ~30 нм; пик ~700 нм (с. 2). Фрагментация: в воде окисление, в ацетоне до 4 нм (FWHM <3 нм), сдвиг 700→640 нм; экстинкция 18→6 л·г⁻¹·см⁻¹ (с. 3). Диапазон лазера — не режим всех опытов; раздел in vitro на с. 3 обрывается.

[источник] Дословные цитаты для сверки:

- «for 100 μJ pulse energy and 5 kHz repetition rate saturation time was 15 min» (с. 2)
- «the increase of pulse energy from 10 to 100 μJ led to the increase of NPs mean diameter from 25 to 40 nm» (с. 2)
- «we observed a drastic decrease in the size of final TiN NPs down to 4 nm» (с. 3)
